La réalisation de cet article s’inscrit: This article follows up on a first report published by La Converse on the circumstances of Nooran Rezayi’s death. For this second instalment, we set out to document the impact of the tragedy on the young people around him.
Le travail de terrain s’est toutefois he: The fieldwork, however, ran into significant obstacles. Several attempts to interview young people who were present the night of the shooting failed. On a few occasions, meetings seemed about to be confirmed before being cancelled at the last minute. Some young people changed their minds along the way, while others, identified as potential witnesses, chose not to speak.
Malgré le recours à de nombreux interméd: Despite going through many intermediaries (community workers, family members, school contacts) and approaching a large number of people, direct access to these accounts remained limited.
Ce contexte a orienté notre travail vers: This led us to focus on interviews with students who agreed to speak anonymously, as well as with psychosocial workers, family members and community actors. The institutions involved, including the Service de police de l’agglomération de Longueuil, were also contacted to give their version of events.
Cette prudence observée sur le terrain f: This caution we encountered on the ground is an integral part of the reality documented in this article.
‍<strong>Six mois après la mort de Noora: ‍Six months after the death of Nooran Rezayi, the Director of Criminal and Penal Prosecutions (DPCP) has yet to decide whether charges will be laid against the police officer involved. Meanwhile, this Thursday, March 19, four mothers are filing a $1.9-million civil suit in Quebec Superior Court on behalf of their five minor children, all of whom were present when 15-year-old Nooran Rezayi was shot dead by police. But while the case makes its way through the courts and institutions, another reality is unfolding on the ground. Outside the teenager’s school, among his friends and in the community organizations supporting them, speech remains fragile. Caught between anger, fear and silence, many young people still carry the trauma of a tragic Sunday whose story remains incomplete.
<l1>La mort de Nooran Rezayi</l1> contin: <l1>The death of Nooran Rezayi</l1> continues to weigh on the young people at the school he attended. And they rarely speak about it. “I hope the officer gets convicted,” says Adam, one of Nooran’s classmates, referring to the report from the Bureau des enquêtes indépendantes (BEI) recently submitted to the Director of Criminal and Penal Prosecutions (DPCP).
Autour de lui, d’autres adolescents acqu: Around him, other teenagers nod in agreement. For them, what’s at stake goes beyond the criminal investigation: it is also a question of trust in institutions. “You never know with this kind of thing […] We don’t even know the officer,” the young man adds. “We just hope justice will be served.”
Dans les couloirs de l’école, les semain: In the school’s hallways, the weeks following Nooran’s death were marked by shock and grief. Psychologists were sent in to support students. But despite that support, some say the wound remains open. “No matter what happens, Nooran is never coming back,” says Claudio, another student.
Sur le terrain, plusieurs intervenants d: On the ground, several community workers describe an emotional climate that has been profoundly shaken among young people since Nooran Rezayi’s death. Jean Neptune, a psychosocial worker in eight secondary schools on the South Shore, sees it too. In his view, violence in schools is not a new phenomenon, but it now seems closer, more visible and more widely covered in the media.
Dans ce contexte déjà fragile, la mort d: In this already fragile context, Nooran’s death has deeply affected teenagers. Many express a feeling of insecurity, sometimes even a direct fear of authorities. “The first time I heard young people tell me they were scared when they saw a patrol car, it hit me,” says Mr. Neptune. Some ask him point-blank: “Am I the next Nooran?”
Avec le recul, l’intervenant affirme qu’: Looking back, the worker says he mainly observes two reactions among the teenagers he supports: anger and fear – emotions that are often closely linked. According to him, “the young people who are very angry are often very scared too.” “They just express it differently,” he sums up.
Si la colère est visible dans l’espace p: While anger is visible in public space, another reaction dominates among many of Nooran’s loved ones: silence. Since the tragedy, psychologist Iman Staali, founder of the Centre de guérison Binetna, has been supporting about twenty young people who were part of his circle of friends.
Selon elle, leur réticence à témoigner p: According to her, their reluctance to speak publicly is not due to a lack of interest, but rather to a climate of fear. “I think it’s a mix of fear and restraint. These aren’t really young people who have the power to freely decide whether to speak,” she explains. “They’re reacting to an environment that frightens them.”
Dans les premiers jours qui ont suivi la: In the first days after the tragedy, the psychologist says she observed intense anger and a desire for justice. But that energy quickly changed. At the vigil held in Nooran’s memory a week after the tragedy, she was struck by the teenagers’ extremely disciplined behaviour. “The young people were saying we shouldn’t shout, shouldn’t make noise, that we had to stay calm,” she says. Even without a significant police presence, many had already absorbed the idea that they had to police themselves.
Pour la psychologue, cette autocensure r: For the psychologist, this self-censorship reveals something deeper. “It’s a form of internalized police violence. As if they had understood that they didn’t even have the right to be angry.”
Sur le terrain, plusieurs témoignages re: On the ground, many accounts gathered from young people, family members and community workers point to the same conclusion: the relationship with police has hardened, and did so well before Nooran Rezayi’s death. And it has hardened even more since the tragedy.
Selon une source parentale, certains jeu: According to a parent source, some young people were allegedly subjected to repeated police interventions after their image circulated publicly. She says these interactions can lead to the creation of police profiles, even in the absence of a criminal record, which, in her view, contributes to a form of persistent surveillance.
Un sentiment partagé par les élèves renc: It’s a feeling shared by the students we met at André-Laurendeau secondary school. “Sometimes the cops are a bit on racialized youth. They’re kind of on our backs,” says Adam, who insists: “We’re not all bad. There’s good and bad in every race, every culture. It’s not because I’m Arab, or he’s Black, or he’s whatever, that we’re bad.”
La psychologue Iman Staali rapporte des: Psychologist Iman Staali reports similar experiences. Several teenagers told her about frequent police stops, before and after the events. These experiences, she says, can have lasting consequences: withdrawal, difficulties at school, even social disengagement. “These are young people who, already at 15, feel pushed aside.”
Le Service de police de la Ville de Mont: The Service de police de la Ville de Montréal, which we contacted, did not respond to our questions about these allegations. The Service de police de l’agglomération de Longueuil (SPAL), for its part, says it has received “no formal complaint” about repeated checks specifically targeting the victim’s loved ones. The police force points out that its interventions are governed by law and that it “does not tolerate any form of racial or social profiling.” It also notes a marked increase in crime among young people, which it says justifies stepped-up prevention and surveillance operations in the area.
Entre ces versions, un écart persiste, d: Between these versions, a gap persists, hard to quantify but very real in the lived experience of young people. Several of those La Converse met believe this gap is measured not only in facts but also in lived experience: that of a strained relationship with institutions at a pivotal point in their lives.
<strong>Binetna et Collectif 15 mars : d: Binetna and Collectif 15 mars: spaces to speak out
La peur, l’isolement et la difficulté à: Fear, isolation and the difficulty of speaking out don’t affect only Nooran Rezayi’s loved ones. These feelings run more widely through families touched by police interventions. This was evident at the<l1> 30</l1><sup><l1>th</l1></sup><l1> International Day Against Police Brutality</l1>, organized by the Collectif 15 mars. The 2026 edition was marked, on March 15, by a demonstration outside the BEI headquarters in Longueuil, calling for justice for Nooran and an end to police brutality.
La veille, plusieurs dizaines de militan: The day before, several dozen activists, researchers and families gathered at the Comité social Centre-Sud in Montréal for a day of discussion. At the heart of the gathering was a space for speaking, intended for the loved ones of people injured or killed in police interventions.
Mais cette parole reste difficile à fair: But getting people to speak remains difficult. Of ten families invited to testify publicly, only two agreed to do so – a figure that in itself speaks to persistent barriers.
Parmi les rares personnes à s’exprimer,: Among the few who spoke, Magda Marshalik did so for the first time. Her father was seriously injured during a police intervention. “It feels good to talk, even if it’s not easy,” she tells La Converse. “We realized we weren’t an isolated case. Many families are going through similar situations.”
Pour elle, ces espaces permettent de rom: For her, these spaces break the isolation and turn an intimate experience into a collective effort: “If we can keep other families from going through things this hard, that’s already a form of power to act.”
Au fil des rencontres, une constante s’i: Over the course of our meetings, one constant emerged: the difficulty of telling the story. Between the cautious accounts outside the school, the silences of loved ones, the stories of community workers and the accusations to which authorities respond with reserve, part of the story still remains out of view.
Six mois après les faits, l’enquête suit: Six months after the events, the investigation is following its course. But for many young people, what’s at stake now goes beyond the legal question alone. It touches their sense of safety, their relationship with institutions and their place in society.
Dans les mots de certains, une même inqu: In some of their words, the same worry keeps coming back, sometimes in a whisper: that of an event that could have happened to them. And of a story that, despite the different versions, remains incomplete.
